acicchakti
(‘non-sentient power [of ब्रह्मन्]’)
------------------------------------------
If the solid world we perceive with our senses is a wonderful phenomenon, the unseen Power behind it is a deep mystery. The quest for the mode by which this unseen Power has evolved into this tangible world has resulted in several philosophical schools, often called ‘darśanas,’ in the text-books of Hindu metaphysics. Of these, the वेदान्त दर्शन of बादरायण has attracted the maximum number of commentators one of whom is निम्बार्क (11th-12th cent. A. D.). According to him, ब्रह्मन्, the highest Reality, is a personal God, identified with कृष्ण or Hari. ब्रह्मन् has two powers cit-शक्ति (sentient power, i.e., the indi-vidual souls) and अचित्-शक्ति (non-sentient power, i.e., nature). At the beginning of च्रेअतिओन्, He manifests these two powers. From अचित्-शक्ति or अचिच्छक्ति, there is a gradual evolution of the entire material world.
This अचिच्छक्ति manifests itself in three different forms:
the prākṛta or what is derived from the प्रकृति, primal matter, responsible for the material world;
the aprākṛta, the non-material aspect, the stuff of the celestial bodies and objects as also the regions where the Lord and the freed souls live;
kāla or time.
See also NIMBĀRKA.

Acintya-bhedābheda School
------------------------------------------
There have always been two major but parallel currents of thought—advocating ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion)—in the Hindu religious tradition, each getting the better of the other at certain periods of history. The school of ज्ञान or knowledge, based on the उपनिषद्स् and allied literature like the darśanas has always stressed that मुक्ति (liberation from transmigratory existence) is possible only through आत्मज्ञान or knowledge of the Self. The school of भक्ति or devotion, rooted in the Ṛgveda, but dependent mainly on the epics and the पुराणस् (mythological lore) has emphasized that such लिबेरतिओन् is possible only through the grace of God, भक्ति or devotion to God being the only means of obtaining it. Each of these two schools, being unable to ignore the logical and psychological force of the other, has been obliged to find a place for some of the principles of the rival school though relegating them to an inferior status. More sober thinkers have attempted at reconciling, even harmonising, these two viewpoints with varying success. The best of such attempts which has succeeded remarkably is found in that classic scripture Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, which itself is based on an earlier work of a similar kind, Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa. The philosophical schools of भक्ति, based on these two and allied works (e.g., Harivaṁśa and Brahmavaivartapurāṇa) could not disregard the उपनिषद्स् or the Brahmasūtras (also called Vedāntasūtras, a work systematising the philosophical ref-lections scattered all over the उपनिषद्स्) which had attained a very high status among thinkers and religious leaders. Hence they ventured to interpret the Brahmasūtras and the उपनिषद्स् by superimposing their views—commonly known as the भागवत school—on them. Though it is difficult to assess the degree of their success, there is no doubt that they have enriched the Hindu philosophical tradition. Among such भागवत schools, those of निम्बार्क (11th-12th cent. A.D.), वल्लभ and श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य or चैतन्य (both of the 15th cent. A. D.) have gained recognition and respectability. The religio-philosophical system propounded by चैतन्य (A.

-1533), जीव गोस्वामी (16th cent. A. D.) and other scholar-mystics of Bengal is known as the Bengal School of वैष्णविस्म्, also designated as the ‘Acintya-bhedābheda’ school. This designation obtains from the fact that the relationship between ब्रह्मन् (God) on the one hand and प्रकृति (nature) and जीव (individual सोउल्) on the other, is ‘acintya’ (incomprehensible) since both ‘bheda’ (difference) and ‘abheda’ (non-difference) can be predicated of it.
The teachings of this school can be summarised briefly as follows: The ultimate Reality is personal, (Brahman or) Śrī कृष्ण, the God of love and grace. He is the same as the ब्रह्मन् of the उपनिषद्स्. He is sat-cit-आनन्द (existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss-absolute). He is infinite, omnipotent and omnipresent. He is the very embodiment of all blessed qualities that we can ever conceive of. In this sense, he is saguṇa (with attributes).
He has three śaktis or powers: स्वरूपशक्ति, māyā-शक्ति and जीव-शक्ति. By his svarūpa-शक्ति (also called cit-शक्ति) he upholds his own existence and that of others, knows and makes others know, enjoys and makes others enjoy bliss. These three characteristics of his svarūpa-शक्ति corresponding to sat, cit and आनन्द aspects of his, are called sandhinī, saṁvit and ह्लादिनी śaktis respectively.
His māyāśakti (also called अचित्-शक्ति or jaḍa-शक्ति), has two aspects: guṇamāyā comprising the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्; jīvamāyā, which makes the jīvas (individual souls) forget their true nature and hence get into the bondage of transmigration. God creates the universe by activating this māyāśakti. The created universe is real but transitory.
All the living beings form his जीव-शक्ति (also called taṭasthaśakti).
Creation proceeds out of him by the exercise of māyāśakti and jīvaśakti. Māyā-शक्ति evolves into the material universe and jīvaśakti involves the jīvas in it. The purpose of च्रेअतिओन् is to give more opportunities for the jīvas to get मुक्ति by striving for it and by working out their कर्म.
God who is the very personification of love and joy, assumes infinite forms including the avatāras or incarnations in this world. Of these, Śrī कृष्ण is the chief. His supreme delight is in love, manifested through the Vṛndāvana-līlā. राधा, the doyen of the गोपीस् and the eternal divine consort of कृष्ण is actually the personification of his hlādinīśakti.
The jīvas who are infinite in number and different from God, are conscious entities atomic in size. They get into the bondage of सṁसार (transmigration) due to the इग्नोरन्चे of their real nature, brought about by māyā. मुक्ति is gained by breaking the bondage of कर्म through भक्ति or devotion to Śrī कृष्ण. This भक्ति can be like that of the servant towards his master (dāsya-भक्ति), that of the friend towards his friend (sakhya-भक्ति), that of the parents towards their child (vātsalya-भक्ति) or that of the beloved towards the lover (kāntā-भक्ति or madhura-भक्ति).
For practising the spiritual disciplines leading to भक्ति, guidance from a competent गुरु (spiritual preceptor) is essential. लोगिच् and reasoning are not to be trusted in the path of religion since they can undermine faith. Ethical virtues like compassion, tranquillity and equani-mity, humility and freedom from passions should be cultivated. Since all devotees are children of God, caste distinctions should be ignored.
When भक्ति matures into an abso-lutely pure and selfless state—called kevalā or śuddhā—the devotee aims exclusively at the loving service of कृष्ण as the nearest and dearest one, for his happiness only and does not care even for मुक्ति. This is posited as the fifth puruṣārtha. (See PURUṢĀRTHAS.)
Though four kinds of मुक्ति (See MOKṢA) like सालोक्य are recognised, the śuddha-भक्त is not interested in them.
All this applies to the jīvas who are bound (baddha). There is another class of jīvas known as nityamuktas (ever-free), who have never been in bondage.
The word ‘acintya-bhedābheda’ itself needs some explanation. Hindu philosophers are broadly divided into two groups, one holding the view that in the ultimate analysis there is no difference (abheda) between ब्रह्मन् and the जीव; and the other accepting difference (bheda). The Bengal school of वैष्णविस्म् differs from both and calls itself ‘acintya-भेदाभेद-वाद,’ since ब्रह्मन् and जीव are identical (abhinna) in some respects and different (bhinna) in others, the very relationship being beyond our comprehension (acintya). Both being cit (consciousness) are identical in that respect. But ब्रह्मन् is vibhu-cit (all-pervading चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्) whereas the जीव is aṇu-cit (atomic चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्). Again, the जीव is an aṁśa (part) of ब्रह्मन् who is the aṁśin (the whole). Since the relation between the part and the whole is one of simultaneous bheda and abheda, the same subsists between ब्रह्मन् and जीव also. How exactly this can be, is beyond human comprehension. Hence the appellation.
On the side of dogma, this school accords Śrī चैतन्य the same status as God since it believes that he is the combined इन्चर्नतिओन् of राधा and कृष्ण.
At the social level, the leaders of this school have contributed significantly by removing caste distinctions and encouraging the cultivation of primary moral and social values.
See also ŚRĪ कृष्ण CAITANYA.

acit
(‘the insentient’)
------------------------------------------
Man is a ‘thinking animal.’ Once his animal needs are satisfied and he obtains relative peace and stability in life, he starts thinking about the ‘how,’ the ‘why’ and the ‘when’ of things perceived. This thinking about the origin and evolution of things has got to be in the form of conjectures and hypotheses before being advanced as theories. Such conjectures and hypotheses again, can start only from the seen and the known before progressing towards the unseen and the unknown. It is but natural that this world in which man lives, moves and has his being (as it were), is the first to catch his attention. Such attention and thinking often leads to a broad categorisation of the created world. Of such categorisations, what can be more simple, direct and obvious than the twofold one, viz., the living and the non-living, the sentient and the non-sentient? This is exactly what the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta system—of which Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) is the chief exponent—has done.
According to this system, the ultimate Reality is threefold: cit (the sentient), अचित् (the insentient) and ईश्वर (God). The former two are dependent realities, subservient to the latter. (For details see VIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.)
The अचित् principle, as its very name indicates, is the matrix of all that is without life and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. Also called प्रकृति (nature), it is jaḍa (lifeless and insentient) but capable of vikāra (modi-fication or evolution). It is अविद्या (ignorance) since it is opposed to true knowledge and also called māyā since it is the cause of all diverse creations. Being insentient it is incapable of evolving by itself but does so under the controlling will of God.
According to one classification this अचित् has three aspects: the śuddha-सत्त्व, the miśra-सत्त्व and सत्त्व-śūnya. The śuddha-सत्त्व aspect has pure सत्त्व गुण (See GUṆAS.) capable of producing knowledge and bliss, and is the matrix out of which the world वैकुण्ठ (See VAIKUṆṬHA.) has been made. It is un-affected by the कर्म of the individual souls and is directly under the control of God. The miśra-सत्त्व aspect has the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्. It is this which evolves as this world, contracts and obstructs the ज्ञान (knowledge) of the jīvas (individual selves) and sustains their bondage by producing viparīta-ज्ञान (knowledge opposed to their real nature). Kāla or time forms the third aspect viz., सत्त्व-śūnya.
Whether kāla should be deemed as an aspect of अचित् or considered as a special power inhering in God has been a point of debate among the thinkers of the Viśiṣṭādvaita school.
